trust.privacy.title: Privacy
trust.privacy.p1: This page explains what happens to data when you use Trust Pack Checker or ask me for a pilot review. The person responsible is Oleksandra Hordieieva; contact details are on the Contact page.
trust.privacy.p2: Files you add are read inside your browser tab. They are not uploaded to any server that I run, and without AI mode no document text leaves the page.
trust.privacy.p3: AI mode is optional and off by default. If you turn it on with your own Anthropic API key and confirm, selected passages are sent from your browser directly to Anthropic's API. Anthropic's own terms and privacy policy apply to that request. I never receive your key or your documents.
trust.privacy.p4: Your browser stores your colour theme, and your API key only if you tick "remember on this device". You can clear both in your browser settings. There are no cookies, analytics or trackers.
trust.privacy.p5: The site is hosted on GitHub Pages. GitHub may log technical data such as IP addresses when the page loads, under GitHub's privacy statement.
trust.privacy.p6: If you write to me, I use your name, email address and the files you choose to send only to do the review and reply. Please remove personal data and confidential commercial terms first. I delete the files after the review and delete our emails when you ask.
trust.privacy.p7: You can ask me what data I hold about you, ask me to correct or delete it, and complain to your data protection authority.
trust.terms.title: Terms of use
trust.terms.p1: Trust Pack Checker is a free tool, provided as it is, without any warranty.
trust.terms.p2: It is not legal advice. Its results are drafts for human review, and its rules have not yet been reviewed by a lawyer. "Found in text" means a passage was found, not that a document meets the law.
trust.terms.p3: Only add documents you are allowed to process. If you use AI mode, you use your own API key and are responsible for its use.
trust.terms.p4: Pilot reviews are manual reviews by me, free of charge, in exchange for honest feedback. They are a completeness check and draft answers, not legal advice. I quote your feedback only with your permission.
trust.terms.p5: I am not liable for decisions made on the basis of the tool's output or a pilot review.

page.about.title: About
page.about.description: Who built Trust Pack Checker and why: an evidence-first DPA and questionnaire checker by Oleksandra Hordieieva.
page.about.p1: I'm Oleksandra Hordieieva. I work in finance at a US telecom company, where my role grew from billing reconciliation into leading GDPR compliance. I am not a lawyer.
page.about.p2: Reconciliation taught me to trust only what can be traced to a source. That is how this tool works: every finding shows the exact quote and page behind it, and when it cannot find one it says "not found in text" instead of guessing.
page.about.p3: The tool is free and runs in your browser. It is tested on synthetic documents, and every miss is published on the main page.

page.art28.title: GDPR Article 28 checklist for processor agreements (DPA)
page.art28.description: The elements GDPR Article 28 requires in a contract between a controller and a processor, in plain words, with what to look for in a DPA and common gaps.
page.art28.intro: Article 28 of the GDPR says what a contract between a controller and a processor must contain. That contract is usually called a data processing agreement (DPA). This checklist lists each element in plain words, what to look for in the text, and why it matters. It is the same list the Trust Pack Checker uses, so the page and the tool never differ.
page.art28.how: Read the DPA with this list next to it. For each element, find the sentence that covers it and note the clause number. If you cannot find a sentence, write "not found in text" rather than assuming it is covered somewhere else.
page.art28.practiceIntro: These points are not listed in Article 28 itself, but they often decide whether a DPA works in practice.
page.art28.gap1: The DPA points to another document (a master agreement, a security annex, the standard contractual clauses) that you do not have. Ask for it: an element covered only by reference is not visible in the text you are reading.
page.art28.gap2: Deletion and return at the end of the service is mentioned, but without saying who chooses between deletion and return, or how long backups are kept.
page.art28.gap3: Audit rights are limited to a report or a certificate, with no way to ask for more information. That may be acceptable, but it should be a decision, not a surprise.
page.art28.gap4: The sub-processor clause allows changes without notice, or gives no way to object.
page.art28.cta: The free checker runs this list against a DPA in your browser and shows the quote behind every element it finds. Try it with the synthetic sample documents first.
guide.notAdvice: Not legal advice. This page explains the text of the law in plain words; it is not a substitute for advice on your contract.

page.questionnaire.title: How to answer a customer security questionnaire without guessing
page.questionnaire.description: A step-by-step, evidence-first way to answer customer security and privacy questionnaires from your own documents, and to mark the gaps honestly.
page.questionnaire.intro: A large customer sends a spreadsheet with a hundred questions about security and data protection, and a deadline. The fastest way to answer is to copy old answers or write what sounds right. The safest way is slower at first: answer only from documents you can show, and mark everything else as a gap. This page describes that evidence-first approach in five steps.
page.questionnaire.s1.title: 1. Collect your documents first
page.questionnaire.s1.body: Before you open the questionnaire, gather the documents your answers will rest on: your DPA template, privacy notice, information security policy, record of processing activities, sub-processor list, incident response plan, and any certificates or audit reports you are allowed to share. Use the current signed-off versions. If a document is a draft, treat it as missing: an answer built on a draft can become untrue the day the draft changes.
page.questionnaire.s2.title: 2. Map each question to a topic
page.questionnaire.s2.body: Questionnaires ask the same things in different words. Group the questions into a small set of topics, such as encryption, access control, sub-processors, international transfers, breach notification, retention and deletion, and audits. For each topic, note which document should answer it. This shows early which topics no document covers, and it keeps answers on the same topic consistent with each other.
page.questionnaire.s3.title: 3. Answer only from evidence
page.questionnaire.s3.body: For each question, find the sentence in your documents that answers it, and quote it with the document name and page or clause. Then write the answer so it says no more than that sentence says. If the policy says data is encrypted at rest, do not answer that it is encrypted at rest and in transit unless another sentence says so. Numbers deserve extra care: breach notice periods, retention periods and response times must match the documents exactly, because the customer may compare your answer with your DPA.
page.questionnaire.s4.title: 4. Mark the gaps honestly
page.questionnaire.s4.body: Some questions will have no supporting sentence. Mark them as gaps instead of filling them in. For each gap, decide one of three things: the answer is true and a document should be updated to say it; the answer needs someone who knows, such as the person who runs your infrastructure; or the honest answer is "no" or "not yet". A clear "not yet, planned for next quarter" is usually received better than a confident answer that a later audit contradicts.
page.questionnaire.s5.title: 5. Get sign-off before you send
page.questionnaire.s5.body: A questionnaire is a written statement to a customer and can become part of the contract. Before it goes out, have the owner of each topic check the answers in their area, and keep a record of who signed off what and on which documents each answer rests. The record makes the next questionnaire faster, because most questions will come back in a different form.
page.questionnaire.why: Answers that are quoted from your own documents can be checked by anyone, including the customer. They stay consistent across questionnaires, and they show where your documents need work. Guessing saves time once; evidence saves time every time the same questions return.
page.questionnaire.cta: Trust Pack Checker maps each question to your own documents in your browser, drafts an answer only when it finds a supporting quote, and lists the gaps. Try it with the synthetic sample questionnaire first.

page.questionnaire.mistakes1: Reusing an old answer without checking that the document it came from has not changed since.
page.questionnaire.mistakes2: Answering "yes" to a question with two parts when the documents support only one of them, for example encryption at rest but not in transit.
page.questionnaire.mistakes3: Giving a breach notice period or a retention period that differs from the one in your DPA. Customers often compare the two.
page.questionnaire.mistakes4: Naming fewer sub-processors than your published list, or naming one that is not on it.
page.questionnaire.mistakes5: Answering "we meet all GDPR requirements". That is a legal conclusion, not a fact your documents can show; describe what you actually do instead, and where it is written down.
